Blue Man Group A New Holiday Surprise Broadway Review

 Author: New York Theater  Published Date: November 18, 2026  Leave a Comment on Blue Man Group A New Holiday Surprise Broadway Review
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:09
Instaread

What may be most surprising about this holiday surprise is how unsurprising it is: The blank blue faces, the splattering and spitting of paint, the marshmallow-catching, the audience conscriptions, the banging on custom-built contraptions that look like a cross between a pipe organ and a radiator, and that function as a cross between a drum and a xylophone. Nothing in this, their Broadway debut (which is also their first holiday tour) would be unfamiliar to anybody who had visited their show at any time during their 34-year residency at Astor Place Theater, which ended in February 2025.   Of course, if they were performing a classic – if “Blue Man Group: A New Holiday Surprise” were the “Hamlet” of wordless avant-garde clowning – then what need would there be to rethink, refresh, regroup?   But while the 90 minutes are stuffed with well-executed stunt and spectacle,  too much of the show feels random, dated,  underdeveloped, or almost perfunctory.  What started four decades ago as edgy performance art by three young artists in the East Village has become an internationally touring entertainment that seems to consider originality far less crucial than quality control.

Before the blue men even appear, for example, we hear a voiceover from a 1950s-style announcer thanking their “generous sponsors” followed by a TV monitor off to the side presentng 1950s style commercial drawings of fictitious products like Thermaserve. Later, there is a more elaborate commercial for a product called Relaxative, and the same clean-cut spokesman offering the 1950s equivalent of public service announcements. This kind of retro-50s satire was the hip and subversive thing to do in the punk 1980s, when Blue Man Group original creators Chris Wink, Matt Goldman and Phil Stanton were starting out. Now it’s retro-retro, or, in other words, just old.

Then there is the audience interaction,  which is extensive and aggressive. Among their signature moves is pelting the audience with streaming paper. In keeping with the holiday theme, their weapons of choice now include candy canes, and monster tree ornaments that they bounce on us like balloons, but  are almost as thick and heavy as soccer balls. At one point, they called a member of the audience to the stage, dressed him in a slick yellow rain suit, put a visor on him, stood him against a blank canvas, and spray painted the front of the rain gear in green paint. Meanwhile, one of the Blue Men drew a tree on the canvas behind him. But something seemed amiss here, because none of the paint sprayed on the man made it to the canvas. (Maybe this was equipment failure? Then could they have improvised and turned the man around, and leaned him against the canvas? One gets the sense that improvisation like that is not in their wheelhouse.)  In another oddly thin encounter, the three called up two women, offered them popcorn, champagne, and separate gifts – one got a snow globe, another a pair of silver handcuffs, which a Blue Man clicked shut, and then reopened. The end.

Advertisement

To package their usual routines into a holiday show, scenic designer Scott Adam Davis has created an elaborate set that looks like an English manor with a decorated fireplace, and ceiling-high picture windows that look out onto a tree-filled garden during a picturesque snowstorm – gorgeous but underutilized. The best use of the holiday theme is the straightforward mini-concert of Christmas melodies that the three Blue Men bang out on their network of white plumbing pipes. In a long-ago burst of creativity, Blue Man Group  forged these PVC pipes into musical instruments of surprisingly resonant timbre and rich texture.

Blue Man Group: A New Holiday Surprise
Lunt-Fontanne Theater through January 3, 2027
Running time: 90 minutes, no intermission
Tickets: $49 – $155
Blue Man Group original creators Chris Wink, Matt Goldman and Phil Stanton
Directed by Matt Ramsey
music director Byron Estep
Scenic design by Scott Adam Davis, lighting design by Michael Atkins, sound design by Richard Phillis, Jr. video design by Mark Comiskey
Featuring: Dan Cooper, Wes Day, Mark Frankel, Alexander Pobutsky, Pete Simpson, Kaylie Brooke, Anastasiya Kostomina
